μεγίστας τῶν πράξεων, καὶ παρὰ θεοῦ τὸ πέρας κατ' εὐδοκίαν εἴτε μὴ δεχόμενας,
ταῖς τῶν ἄστρων περιπλοκαῖς καὶ ταῖς τοιαῖσδε θέσεσι καὶ κινήσεσιν ἐπανατιθείς,

θρανίδος (?) ἀποφάσεσιν.

sections.en:
1 Nicetas Choniates, V, p. 100 P = p. 200, 10, Bonn.: Since he was attributing the most and greatest of actions, and those receiving or not receiving their end from God according to his good pleasure, to the entanglements of the stars and to such positions and motions, and being subjected to the things said by the astrologers equally to the decisions from the throne (?) of God.
2 Nicetas Acominatus Choniates, II, p. 64 A = p. 127, ed. Bonn.
3 Ibid., V, p. 100 A = p. 200, Bonn.
4 Ibid., p. 142 D = p. 199, Bonn.
5 Manuel Acominatus Choniates, p. 63 D = I, p. 126: It seems to almost all those of old and today who have great power that the retrogradations and forward motions of the stars and these positions and such figures of the planets, the approaches and distances and the rest of whatever the astrologers say, contribute to fortunes and the occurrences in human life, speaking falsely against divine providence and secretly introducing fate and the things decreed by necessity as unalterable and unspun.
6 Nicetas, VII, p. 142 D = p. 287, Bonn.

summary.headline: Manuel Comnenus and Astrology
summary.text: Disputation of Emperor Manuel Comnenus and Michael Glycas, describing Manuel’s reliance on astrological signs for military decisions, illness prognostication, and affairs of state, and the court’s fear of predicted storms. It also discusses belief in stellar determinism and introduces John Camaterus as a writer of astrology.
